analysis.one_liner: Speeds up Clean Air Act permits for offshore oil drilling and exempts drilling support vessels from pollution controls.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 253-166 on June 22, 2011, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the Clean Air Act applies to offshore oil and gas drilling. Air quality impacts would be measured only against onshore areas, support vessels serving drilling platforms would be exempt from the platform's emission controls, permit decisions would be due within six months, and EPA's Environmental Appeals Board would lose its power to review these permits. The House passed it; the Senate never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies and their service vessels gain, because they would face a faster, narrower permitting process with fewer emission-control requirements and fewer opportunities for the permit to be challenged or stayed. Coastal residents could see lower retail gasoline prices if more drilling moves ahead, according to the bill's supporters.

how_it_helps.text: Air quality impacts of offshore sources would be measured or modeled 'solely with respect to the impacts in the corresponding onshore area,' narrowing what pollution counts against a drilling permit.

Emissions from vessels servicing offshore drilling sites within 25 miles would still count as the platform's emissions but would not be subject to any emission control requirement applicable to the source.

Permit applications for platform or drill ship exploration would require final agency action within six months, with no EPA Environmental Appeals Board review and administrative stays limited to six months.

analysis.who_pays: People living along coastlines near offshore drilling would bear the cost of air pollution that the current Clean Air Act rules count but this bill would no longer control, including emissions from support vessels and repeated drilling at the same locations. EPA would lose a layer of accountability over offshore permits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities breathing offshore-related air pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts drilling support vessels from emission control requirements and excludes some pollution from what a permit must account for, weakening air quality protections over coastal areas.

By stripping the EPA Environmental Appeals Board of any authority over offshore drilling permits and limiting administrative stays, the bill removes the main internal review channel communities and air agencies have used to challenge offshore permits.
A six-month deadline for final permit action leaves EPA less time to analyze air impacts, and opponents argued during debate that faster permitting does not guarantee lower gasoline prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades weaker air pollution controls and a faster, harder-to-challenge permit process for the prospect of more offshore drilling activity. Supporters framed that as jobs and energy supply; opponents noted it removes pollution accountability with no guaranteed consumer benefit. The costs fall on air quality in coastal areas.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 253-166 on June 22, 2011, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill by a vote of 34-14 on June 2, 2011, and it was reported to the House without amendment on June 16.

On June 22, 2011, a motion to recommit the bill with instructions to require EPA to determine whether pollution control technology for offshore sources lowers retail gasoline prices failed 177-245, with all 177 yes votes from Democrats.
The House passed the bill 253-166: 230 of 239 Republicans voted yes along with 23 of 192 Democrats.
The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where it remained without action until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing Clean Air Act protections for air around offshore drilling stayed in place, including EPA's Environmental Appeals Board review and emission controls for drilling-related activities. Offshore drillers did not get the faster permitting and exemptions the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal air quality rules stayed intact

for.name: Cory Gardner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 26, 2011 and shepherded it to House passage.

for.name: Fred Upton
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Committee held markups June 1-2, ordered the bill reported 34-14, and reported it to the House on June 16.

for.name: 230 of 239 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage (Roll no. 478).

against.name: 164 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage (Roll no. 478); all 177 votes for the motion to recommit requiring a gasoline-price determination came from Democrats.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in June 2011.

against.name: House Democratic amendment sponsors (Speier, Capps, Eshoo, Rush, and others)
against.what_they_did: Offered amendments during House debate on June 22, 2011; each failed on recorded vote demands.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 230 of 239 Republicans voted yes and 23 of 192 Democrats did; the losing motion to recommit drew 177 Democratic votes and zero Republican votes.

industries.note: The bill gives exploratory offshore drilling a six-month permit deadline, removes Environmental Appeals Board review, and narrows what air pollution a permit must cover. The industry's gain is fewer emission-control obligations and fewer ways for its permits to be challenged, which is a cost to coastal air quality.

industries.industry: Marine support and service vessel operators
industries.note: Vessels servicing offshore drilling sites within 25 miles would no longer face emission control requirements tied to the drilling source, reducing their compliance costs while their emissions still count on paper.
The bill strips EPA's Environmental Appeals Board of authority over offshore exploration permits and shortens review timelines, cutting the agency's ability to scrutinize offshore air impacts.
